Adult specimens of Deinosuchus rugosus are estimated to have reached an ultimate total length of 880 centimeters [Li = 880 centimeters], a size that places this species among the largest crocodylomorphs ever to have existed. Skeletal remains from the Campanian deposits of North America suggest that these enormous reptiles achieved a maximum adult body mass of approximately 5,000,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 5,000,000 grams], a value consistent with reconstructions based on femoral circumference scaling relationships in extant crocodilians. This colossal body size would have conferred a clear predatory advantage over large dinosaurs sharing its late Cretaceous riparian habitats. The robust, broad snout and conical teeth of Deinosuchus indicate a feeding ecology that included ambush predation on hadrosaurids and ceratopsians, with bite force estimates derived from skull dimensions suggesting one of the most powerful bites known in archosaurian history. Isotopic analyses of tooth enamel further corroborate a semi-aquatic lifestyle, with oxygen isotope ratios reflecting significant time spent in freshwater environments, though some evidence hints at occasional excursions into estuarine systems.

Understanding the growth dynamics of Deinosuchus rugosus has required paleohistological interpretation of long bone sections, which reveal annual growth rings comparable to those observed in modern crocodilians. Based on such analyses, the maximum lifespan for this species has been estimated at approximately 18,615 days [am = approximately 18,615 days] when considering an average thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], though these figures remain speculative given the fragmentary nature of the fossil record. The depositional rate of lines of arrested growth suggests that individuals grew rapidly during early ontogeny before reaching a plateau in later life stages, a pattern also observed in extant large-bodied crocodylians such as Crocodylus porosus. Skeletochronological data further imply that Deinosuchus maintained determinate growth after reaching skeletal maturity, with consecutive growth marks in older specimens becoming increasingly compressed. This prolonged growth trajectory would have required substantial energy acquisition over several decades, likely facilitated by a generalist diet and low metabolic costs typical of ambush predators.

Reproductive biology in Deinosuchus rugosus is necessarily inferred from the anatomy and nesting ecology of extant crocodylomorphs, as no direct fossilized nests or eggs have been definitively assigned to this taxon. Given its large body size, females would likely have laid numerous eggs per nesting event, with the maximum reproductive rate hypothesized to be approximately 0.55 offspring per day under a stable thermal environment of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a speculative estimate derived from allometric scaling of cumulative neonate output relative to adult body mass. Nest construction would probably have involved mound-building with vegetative material, as seen in most modern crocodilians, where incubation temperature influences offspring sex ratio. The immense size of adult females would have permitted investment in relatively large clutch masses, though the absence of direct fossil evidence means such parameters remain subject to revision as future discoveries emerge. Nevertheless, the energetic demands of producing such a large number of offspring over a breeding season would have required abundant prey resources and access to warm, stable nesting sites.

The onset of sexual maturity in Deinosuchus rugosus is thought to have occurred at a substantial age, consistent with the general correlation between large adult body size and delayed reproductive maturation observed across reptiles. Based on extrapolations from growth ring counts and comparisons with extant giant crocodylians, the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 10,950 days [tp = 10,950 days] at a mean ambient temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], though this figure carries considerable uncertainty due to the paucity of juvenile specimens in the fossil record. Reaching reproductive size so late in life would have imposed a high demographic risk, as mortality before first breeding would have severely limited recruitment into the breeding population. This protracted juvenile period likely selected for intense maternal care, including guarding of nest sites and possible post-hatching protection of young, behaviors documented in several extant crocodilian species with similarly delayed maturation. The combination of late maturity, large body size, and high fecundity suggests a life-history strategy balancing slow generation times with high per-offspring survival potential.

Comparative life-history analyses of Deinosuchus rugosus reveal a suite of demographic features that align it with the slow end of the reptilian fast-slow continuum. Its remarkable ultimate length of 880 centimeters [Li = 880 centimeters] and a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 5,000,000 grams [Wwi = 5,000,000 grams] place it in a body size category occupied by only a handful of aquatic amniotes, such as pliosaurid plesiosaurs and some large marine mammals. When placed alongside related alligatoroids from the same geological period, Deinosuchus exhibits a substantially higher growth rate during the pre-reproductive phase, likely fueled by endothermic-like metabolic capacity inferred from bone histology. The ecological role of this apex predator appears to have been that of a dominant consumer within its late Cretaceous ecosystem, exerting top-down control on various aquatic and terrestrial prey species. Given the thermoregulatory challenges faced by such a large ectotherm, the species likely inhabited relatively warm low-latitude waterways, where sustained temperatures supported its elevated growth and digestive efficiency. The eventual extinction of Deinosuchus at the end of the Campanian remains incompletely understood but may relate to sea-level regression and associated habitat fragmentation.
